sections.h2: Does insurance cover wisdom teeth removal?
sections.html:
Most dental insurance plans cover wisdom teeth removal when it is needed, typically paying about 50% to 80% of the total cost, according to Delta Dental. Simple extractions of erupted teeth are often basic services; surgical removal of impacted teeth may fall under oral surgery, with its own percentage.

Your share depends on how your plan classifies the procedure, your deductible, your remaining annual maximum and whether the oral surgeon is in network. Check your benefits summary under extractions and oral surgery.

sections.h2: How do you estimate your cost with insurance?
sections.html:
You can estimate wisdom teeth removal cost with insurance by applying your plan's terms to the surgeon's fees.

  1. Get an itemised quote listing each tooth, the extraction type, imaging and sedation.
  2. Subtract any unmet deductible.
  3. Apply the coverage percentage for each item.
  4. Check your remaining annual maximum; four surgical extractions can approach or exceed it.
  5. Add any items the plan excludes, such as certain sedation.

The surgeon's office can submit a pre-treatment estimate so your insurer confirms what it will pay.

sections.h2: What does wisdom teeth removal cost before insurance?
sections.html:
Before insurance, wisdom teeth removal costs about $720 for all four erupted teeth removed non-surgically, $550 per tooth for one surgical extraction, and $3,120 for all four removed surgically with sedation or anesthesia, based on Delta Dental's out-of-network averages.

CareCredit reports $835 for a single impacted wisdom tooth and $3,340 for four impacted teeth. See our main wisdom teeth removal cost guide for details.

sections.h2: Does insurance cover sedation for wisdom teeth?
sections.html:
Insurance coverage for sedation during wisdom teeth removal varies. Local anesthetic is included in the extraction fee. IV sedation and general anesthesia are often covered for surgical removal of impacted teeth, but some plans limit or exclude them, or cover them only when deemed medically necessary.

Ask your insurer specifically about anesthesia codes before surgery. If sedation is not covered, ask the surgeon what it will cost and whether local anesthetic with nitrous oxide is a suitable alternative for your case.

sections.h2: Can medical insurance pay for wisdom teeth removal?
sections.html:
Medical insurance sometimes pays for wisdom teeth removal, especially for deeply impacted teeth, removal in a hospital setting, or complications such as cysts or infections. Coverage rules differ widely between medical plans.

Some oral surgery offices bill medical insurance first and dental insurance second. Ask the surgeon's office whether they can check both and coordinate benefits.

sections.h2: Will removing all four teeth use up your annual maximum?
sections.html:
Removing all four wisdom teeth, especially surgically with sedation, can use up a large share of your annual maximum. If the plan's share exceeds what is left, you pay the difference.

If the teeth are not urgent, some people split treatment across two benefit years. This means two surgeries and two recoveries, so weigh the savings against the inconvenience and extra sedation costs.

sections.h2: Is there a waiting period for wisdom teeth removal?
sections.html:
Many dental plans have waiting periods for oral surgery or basic services, often several months. During that time, wisdom teeth removal may not be covered.

If your wisdom teeth are causing pain or infection, waiting may not be safe. Ask your dentist whether removal can be delayed and compare the self-pay cost now with your expected share later. See wisdom teeth pain for warning signs.

sections.h2: Does insurance require wisdom teeth to be problematic?
sections.html:
Some insurance plans require evidence that wisdom teeth removal is necessary, such as X-rays showing impaction, decay, infection or damage to neighbouring teeth. Removal of healthy, symptom-free wisdom teeth may be questioned by some plans.

The Cleveland Clinic's wisdom teeth removal guide and its impacted wisdom teeth guide explain common reasons for removal.

sections.h2: What should you budget for recovery?
sections.html:
Recovery costs are usually small: pain relievers, ice packs, soft foods and possibly time off. Follow-up visits are often included in the surgeon's fee.

Dry socket, the most common complication, may need extra visits; the Cleveland Clinic explains prevention. Plan with our wisdom teeth recovery timeline and what to eat after wisdom teeth removal.

sections.h2: Does choosing an in-network oral surgeon matter?
sections.html:
Choosing an in-network oral surgeon matters because in-network providers accept your plan's negotiated fees, which are usually lower than their standard fees, and they cannot bill you above that amount for covered services. Your share is then calculated on the lower negotiated fee.

Out-of-network surgeons may charge more than your plan considers reasonable. The plan pays its percentage of its own allowed amount, and you may owe the difference, which can be significant for surgical removal with sedation. Before booking, confirm the surgeon's network status with both the office and your insurer.

sections.h2: How do you get an accurate estimate before surgery?
sections.html:
To get an accurate estimate before wisdom teeth surgery, ask the surgeon's office for a pre-treatment estimate listing every code: the consultation, panoramic X-ray or 3D scan, each extraction by type, and the anesthesia. The office sends this to your insurer, which replies with its expected payment.

Also ask whether the office checks medical insurance, whether post-operative visits are included, and how they bill if a tooth turns out to be more complex than expected. Having these answers in writing helps avoid surprise bills after surgery.

sections.h2: What if you do not have insurance?
sections.html: If you do not have insurance, compare the costs above with self-pay options at dental schools, community clinics and practices that offer payment plans. See our guide to wisdom teeth removal costs without insurance for savings ideas.

sections.h2: Can you time wisdom teeth removal around your benefit year?
sections.html: You can sometimes time wisdom teeth removal around your benefit year if the teeth are not causing problems. Having surgery early in a new benefit year means your full annual maximum is available, rather than what is left after other treatment. If you need other major work, such as crowns, planning the order across benefit years can help you get the most from your coverage. Never delay removal of painful or infected teeth for benefit timing.

faq.q: How much is wisdom teeth removal with insurance?
faq.a: With insurance, wisdom teeth removal is typically covered at about 50% to 80% of the total cost, according to Delta Dental, so your share depends on your plan. Before insurance, Delta Dental's averages are $720 for four erupted teeth and $3,120 for four surgical with sedation.

faq.q: Does dental insurance cover wisdom teeth removal?
faq.a: Most dental insurance plans cover medically necessary wisdom teeth removal, often as basic or oral surgery services. Coverage percentages, deductibles, annual maximums and waiting periods affect what you pay.

faq.q: Does insurance cover anesthesia for wisdom teeth removal?
faq.a: Insurance often covers IV sedation or general anesthesia for surgical removal of impacted wisdom teeth, but some plans limit or exclude it. Local anesthetic is included in the extraction fee. Check with your insurer before surgery.

faq.q: Can medical insurance cover wisdom teeth removal?
faq.a: Medical insurance sometimes covers wisdom teeth removal, especially for deeply impacted teeth, hospital-based surgery or complications such as cysts. Ask the oral surgeon's office to check both medical and dental coverage.

faq.q: Will removing four wisdom teeth max out my insurance?
faq.a: Removing four wisdom teeth surgically with sedation can use a large share of your annual maximum, and you pay any amount above it. A pre-treatment estimate shows how much your plan will pay.
